chapters.title: Chapter 1: Federal Pleading and Rule 12(b)(6) Dismissals
chapters.description: Explains how federal courts evaluate complaints at the motion-to-dismiss stage and when dismissal is appropriate.
subtopics: Rule 8(a) and the plausibility standard (Twombly/Iqbal)
Rule 12(b)(6) framework and what must be accepted as true
Affirmative defenses resolved on the pleadings when apparent on the face of the complaint
Consideration of exhibits and documents incorporated by reference
Judicial notice of public records (including copyright registrations)
Leave to amend and futility

chapters.title: Chapter 2: Federal Appellate Review of 12(b)(6) Rulings
chapters.description: Covers when and how federal courts of appeals review dismissals for failure to state a claim.
subtopics: Final judgment rule and appealability
De novo standard of review for Rule 12(b)(6) dismissals
Scope of the appellate record
Affirmance on any ground supported by the record
Harmless error and alternative holdings

chapters.title: Chapter 3: Copyright Law—Core Statutory Framework
chapters.description: Introduces the Copyright Act’s basic concepts and rights relevant to infringement and defenses.
subtopics: Subject matter of copyright and fixation (17 U.S.C. § 102)
Ownership and authorship; works made for hire
Exclusive rights (17 U.S.C. § 106)
Registration and § 411(a) prerequisite to suit; effect of registration
Definitions, including “publication” (17 U.S.C. § 101)
Available remedies and defenses overview

chapters.title: Chapter 4: Fair Use—Structure, Policy, and Burdens
chapters.description: Provides an overview of the § 107 fair use doctrine and its flexible, context-dependent application.
subtopics: Statutory text and non-exhaustive list of purposes (criticism, comment, news reporting, etc.)
The four statutory factors and holistic balancing
Burden of proof and the nature of the defense
Commerciality and its non-dispositive role
Licensing markets versus socially valuable secondary uses

chapters.title: Chapter 5: Factor One—Purpose and Character of Use After Warhol
chapters.description: Explores the modern analysis of transformative use and the objective assessment of purpose.
subtopics: Transformative use and “adds something new, with a further purpose or different character”
Objective reasonable-observer perspective on purpose
Parody, satire, commentary, and criticism distinctions
Relevance (and limits) of good or bad faith in fair use
Commercial motivation weighed against transformative character

chapters.title: Chapter 6: Factors Two and Three—Nature of the Work and Amount Taken
chapters.description: Details how courts assess the kind of work used and the quantity/quality of the taking.
subtopics: Factual versus creative works; unpublished versus published status
How publication status affects factor two
Quantitative and qualitative substantiality (“heart of the work”)
Necessity of the amount taken to achieve the secondary purpose
Use of complete works in commentary and parody contexts

chapters.title: Chapter 7: Factor Four—Market Effect and Usurpation
chapters.description: Explains how courts evaluate market harm and the difference between substitution and criticism.
subtopics: Actual and potential markets considered under factor four
Usurpation of traditional, reasonable, or likely-to-develop licensing markets
Why harm from criticism, parody, or ridicule is not cognizable market harm
Evidence and presumptions concerning market substitution
Derivative markets versus transformative markets

chapters.title: Chapter 8: Resolving Fair Use at the Pleading Stage
chapters.description: Describes when courts decide fair use on a motion to dismiss based on the complaint and incorporated materials.
subtopics: Considering the works themselves on a motion to dismiss
Incorporation by reference of audiovisual works and transcripts
Judicial notice and the role of undisputed authenticity
Limits on resolving factual disputes versus legal inferences
Appellate review of pleading-stage fair use determinations

chapters.title: Chapter 9: Copyright Act § 301 Preemption of State-Law Claims
chapters.description: Outlines the preemption test for state-law claims that overlap with copyright rights.
subtopics: Two-prong § 301 test: subject matter and equivalency of rights
The “extra element” or “qualitative difference” doctrine
Preemption and breach of contract, implied contract, and fraud claims
Drafting around preemption with independent contractual promises
Remedial implications of preemption determinations

chapters.title: Chapter 10: Third-Party Beneficiaries and Online Terms—Illinois Law
chapters.description: Covers when nonparties may enforce contracts under Illinois law, with emphasis on platform Terms of Service.
subtopics: Intended versus incidental beneficiaries
Strong presumption against third-party enforcement
Requirement of clear or express declaration of intent to benefit
Application to clickwrap/browsewrap/platform agreements
Interplay with choice-of-law clauses and forum selection

chapters.title: Chapter 11: Implied-in-Fact Contracts—New York Law
chapters.description: Explains formation and enforcement of implied-in-fact agreements under New York law.
subtopics: Assent inferred from conduct; consideration
Essential terms must be definite and pleaded with specificity
Meeting of the minds and objective manifestations
Distinguishing implied-in-fact from quasi-contract/unjust enrichment
Pleading standards for implied agreements in entertainment/media contexts

chapters.title: Chapter 12: Fraudulent Inducement—Elements and Damages in New York
chapters.description: Sets out the elements of fraudulent inducement and New York’s distinctive damages rule.
subtopics: Material misrepresentation, scienter, intent, justifiable reliance, causation
Out-of-pocket loss rule versus benefit-of-the-bargain damages
Consequential and incidental losses cognizable in fraud
Interaction with Rule 9(b) particularity pleading
Economic loss and duplicative-claim concerns

chapters.title: Chapter 13: State Law Choice-of-Law in Federal Copyright Suits
chapters.description: Addresses how federal courts select governing state law for supplemental contract and tort claims.
subtopics: Supplemental jurisdiction over state claims in federal-question cases
Erie doctrine and forum state choice-of-law rules
Enforcement of contractual choice-of-law clauses
Determining governing law for tort versus contract claims
Effect on elements, defenses, and remedies

chapters.title: Chapter 14: Landmark Fair Use Precedents—Campbell, Authors Guild, Cariou, TCA, and Hachette
chapters.description: Surveys key fair use decisions that shape modern doctrine, especially in the Second Circuit.
subtopics: Campbell v. Acuff-Rose Music, Inc.: parody, commercial use, and factor-four analysis
Authors Guild v. Google, Inc.: transformative search and non-substitutive uses
Cariou v. Prince: appropriation art and assessing transformation by examining the works
TCA Television Corp. v. McCollum: resolving fair use at the Rule 12(b)(6) stage
Hachette Book Group, Inc. v. Internet Archive: market usurpation versus harm from criticism and the flexible fair use inquiry

chapters.title: Chapter 15: Landmark New York Fraud Damages—Lama Holding and Progeny
chapters.description: Explains New York’s out-of-pocket measure for fraud damages and its implications for pleading and proof.
subtopics: Lama Holding Co. v. Smith Barney Inc.: out-of-pocket loss as the exclusive measure
Prohibition on benefit-of-the-bargain in fraud claims
Causation and proof of pecuniary loss
Interaction with contract remedies and election of remedies
Practical pleading strategies to allege recoverable losses
